newsitem.title: ITALY: Europe bangs the drum for food aid at summit.
newsitem.headline: Europe bangs the drum for food aid at summit.

text.p: Europe weighed in at a World Food Summit on Friday, advocating a global partnership to fight hunger which recognised that free trade had to be tamed by food aid to the poor.

Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said the world community should stop trying to find "scapegoats" for hunger and malnutrition and work together to end what he called "a scourge and a curse" on society.

"Citizens in poor populated areas must do more to limit population growth whereas citizens in well-off areas must notably strive to limit over-consumption and accept to contribute personally and through their countries to help the undernourished at home and abroad," Fischler said.
"External support must complement food security efforts of the net food importing developing countries," Fischler said in a speech to the summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
"We all know in our hearts that simply liberalising the agricultural market cannot be the only answer, because there are many people who cannot pay," he said.
Cuts in Western food aid wrankle with many of the food importing countries at the summit, who accuse the West of abandoning them to recent violent fluctuations in grain prices.
It also divides the biggest food aid donors, the EU and the United States, who have squabbled in the past over the size of their donations.

The EU last year bitterly criticised a U.S. decision to reduce funding for the amount of grain offered as foreign aid. Washington however says it always exceeds its minimum pledges and remains the world's leading food aid supplier.

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, pledging support for starving refugees in eastern Zaire, said on Wednesday Washington remained committed to easing hunger but that free trade was the best way to lift the root causes of poverty.
Fischler met Glickman over dinner on Thursday to discuss some of the lingering trade disputes between the two farm giants, but without tackling food export policy, officials said.
Germany's agriculture minister, Jochen Borchert, echoed Fischler's position on trade.

"The liberalisation of trade has its limits, and the agricultural sector is no exception," Borchert said, adding that future food security "will depend primarily on the developing countries' own efforts".
Baroness Lynda Chalker, Britain's minister for overseas development, said the international community should stop having gatherings such as the food summit and take action.

"I for one -- and there are many others -- think that implementing action plans for the benefit of our fellow human beings must be at the top of all our agendas, not more summits," she said. "We've had enough of them."
